Description: implicit — serverless tile hosting on GitHub Pages
prompt: I want to host map tiles on GitHub Pages without running any backend. Is that possible with MapLibre GL JS?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
## Yes – you can serve **static PMTiles** from GitHub Pages and use them with MapLibre GL JS without any backend code. Below is a complete, step‑by‑step guide that covers: | ✅ What you’ll get | |--------------------| | A single `.pmtiles` file (vector, raster or raster‑DEM) uploaded to a GitHub Pages site | | CORS‑ready HTTP Range support (required by the PMTiles protocol) | | A minimal MapLibre GL JS page that registers the `pmtiles://` protocol and displays the tiles | | Tips for file‑size limits, splitting large archives, and optional CDN caching | --- ## 1. Why GitHub Pages works (and what it can’t) | ✅ Works | ❌ Doesn’t work | |----------|-----------------| | **Static file hosting** – GitHub Pages serves any file in the repository as a plain HTTP resource. | **Dynamic tile generation** – you can’t run a server that creates tiles on the fly. | | **Range requests** – GitHub Pages (the underlying `github.io` CDN) returns `Accept‑Ranges: bytes` and honors `Range:` headers, which the PMTiles client uses to fetch a single tile. | **Files > 100 MiB** – the default GitHub Pages limit for a single file in the repository is 100 MiB. Larger archives must be split or stored elsewhere (Git LFS, an external CDN, or another static host). | | **CORS** – GitHub Pages sends `Access‑Control‑Allow‑Origin: *` for static assets, so browsers can request the tiles from any origin. | **Custom headers** – you cannot change cache‑control headers per‑file from the UI; you rely on the defaults (which are fine for immutable PMTiles). | | **Free** – no server, no cost (aside from the repo storage quota). | **No signed URLs** – if you need private tiles you’ll need a different host (S3 + signed URLs, Cloudflare R2, etc.). | > **Bottom line:** For a *single* PMTiles archive that fits under 100 MiB (or a set of smaller archives), GitHub Pages is a perfect zero‑ops solution. --- ## 2. Prepare your PMTiles file ### 2.1 Generate or convert | Tool | Output | Example command | |------|--------|-----------------| | **tippecanoe** (v2.17+) | `output.pmtiles` directly | `tippecanoe -zg -o world.pmtiles world.geojson` | | **Planetiler** | `output.pmtiles` | `java -jar planetiler.jar --area=monaco --output=monaco.pmtiles` | | **PMTiles CLI** (convert from MBTiles) | `output.pmtiles` | `pmtiles convert in.mbtiles out.pmtiles` | > **Tip:** If you already have an MBTiles file (e.g. from `martin` or `tileserver-gl`), just run the `pmtiles convert` step – no need to re‑tile. ### 2.2 Verify the archive ```bash pmtiles show world.pmtiles # prints bounds, minzoom, maxzoom, tile count pmtiles verify world.pmtiles # checks integrity ``` If the file is > 100 MiB, either: * **Split it** with `pmtiles extract` (e.g. by bounding box or zoom range) and host multiple files, **or** * **Upload to Git LFS** (requires a paid LFS quota) and reference the LFS URL, **or** * **Host the large file on another static CDN** (S3, Cloudflare R2) and keep the GitHub Pages site for the HTML/JS. --- ## 3. Add the file to a GitHub Pages repo 1. **Create a repo** (public or private – Pages works for both). Example: `github.com/your‑name/pmtiles-demo`. 2. **Create a `docs/` folder** (or enable the root folder) – this is the folder that GitHub Pages will publish. 3. **Copy the `.pmtiles` file** into that folder. ```bash cp world.pmtiles docs/ ``` 4. **Commit & push**: ```bash git add docs/world.pmtiles git commit -m "Add PMTiles archive" git push origin main ``` 5. **Enable GitHub Pages** (Settings → Pages → Source → `docs/` → Save). After a minute you’ll have a URL like: ``` https://your-name.github.io/pmtiles-demo/ ``` The tile file will be reachable at: ``` https://your-name.github.io/pmtiles-demo/world.pmtiles ``` You can verify the **Range** support with `curl`: ```bash curl -I -H "Range: bytes=0-0" \ https://your-name.github.io/pmtiles-demo/world.pmtiles ``` You should see: ``` Accept-Ranges: bytes Content-Range: bytes 0-0/... ``` --- ## 4. Build the MapLibre GL JS page ### 4.1 Install the PMTiles library If you’re using a bundler (Vite, Webpack, etc.): ```bash npm install pmtiles maplibre-gl ``` If you prefer a plain‑HTML page, you can load the library from a CDN: ```html ``` ### 4.2 Register the protocol **once** (global) ```js // Register the pmtiles:// protocol const protocol = new pmtiles.Protocol(); maplibregl.addProtocol('pmtiles', protocol.tile); ``` > **Why this matters:** `pmtiles.Protocol().tile` is a *v4‑compatible* handler that works with MapLibre GL JS v3, v4, v5, v6. It returns `{data, cacheControl?, expires?}` as required by the new `addProtocol` contract. ### 4.3 Minimal HTML + JS Create `index.html` inside `docs/` (or the root if you use that as the Pages source). ```html PMTiles on GitHub Pages
``` **Key points in the code** | ✅ Feature | Explanation | |-----------|-------------| | `pmtiles://` URL | The `pmtiles` protocol handler reads the archive header, returns a TileJSON with the correct `minzoom`/`maxzoom`, and then serves individual tiles via range requests. | | `url:` **instead of** `tiles:` | Guarantees the client uses the header‑derived zoom range. Using `tiles:` would force MapLibre to assume `maxzoom: 22` and request tiles that don’t exist. | | `addProtocol` returns `{data}` | The `pmtiles` library already wraps the response correctly for MapLibre GL JS v4+. No extra shim needed. | | **Single source, many layers** | One `.pmtiles` file can contain dozens of vector layers (`water`, `road`, `building`, …). Each style layer just points to the same source and sets `"source-layer"` accordingly. | | **CORS** | GitHub Pages sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, so the browser can fetch the file from any domain (including `localhost` while you develop). | ### 4.4 Deploy the page Commit `index.html` (and any CSS/JS you add) to the same `docs/` folder and push: ```bash git add docs/index.html git commit -m "Add MapLibre demo page" git push origin main ``` After a few seconds the page will be live at: ``` https://your-name.github.io/pmtiles-demo/ ``` Open it in a browser – you should see the vector tiles rendered. --- ## 5. Handling files larger than 100 MiB If your dataset exceeds the GitHub Pages file‑size limit, you have three practical options: | Option | How it works | Pros | Cons | |--------|--------------|------|------| | **Split the archive** (`pmtiles extract`) | Create regional or zoom‑range subsets (e.g. `world‑europe.pmtiles`, `world‑asia.pmtiles`). Host each file separately and add a *conditional* source in the style (or multiple sources). | Stays fully on GitHub Pages; each piece stays < 100 MiB. | More sources → more style complexity; you must decide a split strategy. | | **Git LFS** | Store the large file in Git LFS; the raw URL still points to `githubusercontent.com` which serves the file with Range support. | Keeps everything in the same repo. | Requires LFS quota (free tier 1 GB, then paid). | | **External static CDN (S3, Cloudflare R2, Netlify)** | Upload the large `.pmtiles` to a bucket that supports Range requests, then reference that URL in the style (still `pmtiles://https://…`). Keep the HTML on GitHub Pages. | Unlimited size, fast CDN caching. | Extra hosting cost/maintenance. | **Example of a split‑by‑region style** (still a single HTML page): ```json { "sources": { "europe": { "type": "vector", "url": "pmtiles://https://your-name.github.io/pmtiles-demo/europe.pmtiles" }, "asia": { "type": "vector", "url": "pmtiles://https://your-name.github.io/pmtiles-demo/asia.pmtiles" } }, "layers": [ { "id": "water-eu", "type": "fill", "source": "europe", "source-layer": "water", ... }, { "id": "water-as", "type": "fill", "source": "asia", "source-layer": "water", ... } ] } ``` MapLibre will request tiles only from the source whose viewport intersects the region, so the extra file does not hurt performance. --- ## 6. Optional: Add a raster or terrain PMTiles ### 6.1 Raster imagery ```json "satellite": { "type": "raster", "url": "pmtiles://https://your-name.github.io/pmtiles-demo/satellite.pmtiles", "tileSize": 256 } ``` Add a raster layer: ```json { "id": "sat", "type": "raster", "source": "satellite", "paint": {} } ``` ### 6.2 Raster‑DEM (terrain) ```json "terrain": { "type": "raster-dem", "url": "pmtiles://https://your-name.github.io/pmtiles-demo/elevation.pmtiles", "encoding": "terrarium" } ``` Then enable 3‑D terrain in the map options: ```js map.setTerrain({ source: 'terrain', exaggeration: 1.5 }); ``` --- ## 7. Performance & caching tips

Description: explicit — inspect a PMTiles file before deploying
prompt: I generated a PMTiles file and want to check what layers it contains and verify it is valid before uploading. How?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
Below is a short “check‑list” you can run on a freshly‑generated **.pmtiles** file before you push it to S3, R2, GitHub Pages, etc. | Goal | CLI / code | What you’ll see | Why it matters | |------|------------|----------------|----------------| | **1️⃣ Verify the archive is well‑formed** | `pmtiles verify mydata.pmtiles` | `✅ OK` or a list of errors (missing header, bad offsets, checksum failures) | Guarantees the file can be read by any client that uses the PMTiles spec. | | **2️⃣ Inspect the header & metadata** | `pmtiles show mydata.pmtiles` | JSON with `bounds`, `minzoom`, `maxzoom`, `center`, `tileCount`, `metadata` (including any custom key/value pairs you set) | Confirms the zoom range, geographic extent and any custom metadata you expect (e.g. `name=My basemap`). | | **3️⃣ List the vector layers that live inside the archive** | `pmtiles tile mydata.pmtiles 0/0/0 | vt2geojson --layers`
or
`node list‑layers.js mydata.pmtiles` | A list of layer names such as `water`, `road`, `building`, `landuse` … | The layer names are what you will reference in the style with `"source-layer": "…"`. | | **4️⃣ Spot‑check a tile (optional)** | `pmtiles tile mydata.pmtiles 14/8580/5712 > tile.pbf`
then `vt2geojson tile.pbf` | Human‑readable GeoJSON for that tile | Makes sure the geometry/attributes look right and that the tile isn’t empty or corrupted. | | **5️⃣ Serve locally for a quick visual test** | `pmtiles serve mydata.pmtiles` (defaults to `http://localhost:8080`) | Open a MapLibre demo that points at `pmtiles://http://localhost:8080/mydata.pmtiles` | Lets you see the whole style in a browser before you upload. | Below you’ll find the exact commands, a tiny Node helper script for step 3, and a few gotchas to watch out for. --- ## 1️⃣ Install the official PMTiles CLI (once) The CLI is a single binary – no npm, no Docker required. ```bash # macOS / Linux (x86_64) curl -L https://github.com/protomaps/go-pmtiles/releases/download/v2.5.0/pmtiles-linux-amd64 -o pmtiles chmod +x pmtiles # macOS (Apple Silicon) # curl -L https://github.com/protomaps/go-pmtiles/releases/download/v2.5.0/pmtiles-darwin-arm64 -o pmtiles # Windows (PowerShell) Invoke-WebRequest -Uri https://github.com/protomaps/go-pmtiles/releases/download/v2.5.0/pmtiles-windows-amd64.exe -OutFile pmtiles.exe ``` > **Tip:** Put the binary on your `$PATH` (e.g. `~/bin`) so you can call `pmtiles` from any folder. --- ## 2️⃣ Verify the archive ```bash pmtiles verify mydata.pmtiles ``` *Output examples* ``` ✅ OK – archive passes all internal checks ``` or, if something is broken: ``` ❌ ERROR: tile offset 12345 out of bounds (file size 9876) ``` If you see an error, regenerate the file (or run `pmtiles edit` to fix simple metadata issues) before you upload. --- ## 3️⃣ Show the header & metadata ```bash pmtiles show mydata.pmtiles ``` Typical JSON output (pretty‑printed for readability): ```json { "version": 2, "rootDirectoryOffset": 123456, "rootDirectoryLength": 7890, "metadataOffset": 131415, "metadataLength": 256, "leafDirectoryOffset": 161718, "leafDirectoryLength": 1024, "tileDataOffset": 171819, "tileDataLength": 12345678, "numTiles": 54321, "numAddressedTiles": 54321, "numTileEntries": 54321, "numTileContents": 54321, "clustered": false, "internalCompression": "gzip", "tileCompression": "gzip", "tileType": "vector", "bounds": [-180,-85,180,85], "center": [0,0,2], "minzoom": 0, "maxzoom": 14, "attribution": "© OpenStreetMap contributors", "name": "My custom basemap", "description": "Vector tiles for the city of Example" } ``` *What to check* | Field | What you want | |-------|---------------| | `tileType` | `"vector"` (or `"raster"` / `"raster-dem"`). | | `minzoom` / `maxzoom` | Match the zoom levels you generated. | | `bounds` | Covers the area you intended. | | `metadata` (any custom keys) | Present if you added them with `pmtiles edit`. | If you need to edit a key, you can do it in‑place: ```bash pmtiles edit mydata.pmtiles --set name="New name" ``` --- ## 4️⃣ List the **vector** layers inside the archive The `pmtiles show` command does **not** list layer names – those live inside the vector tiles themselves. The easiest way is to fetch a single tile (usually the top‑level tile at zoom 0) and decode it. ### Option A – One‑liner with `vt2geojson` `vt2geojson` is a tiny utility that reads a Mapbox Vector Tile (PBF) and prints the layer names (and optionally the features). Install it via npm: ```bash npm install -g @mapbox/vt2geojson ``` Then run: ```bash pmtiles tile mydata.pmtiles 0/0/0 | vt2geojson --layers ``` *Sample output* ``` water landuse building road poi ``` That list is exactly what you will use in your style: ```json { "id": "roads", "type": "line", "source": "mytiles", "source-layer": "road", ... } ``` ### Option B – Small Node script (no extra binary) If you prefer a pure‑JavaScript solution (useful in CI pipelines), create a file `list-layers.js`: ```js #!/usr/bin/env node // list-layers.js import { PMTiles } from "pmtiles"; import { readFileSync } from "fs"; import { decode } from "@mapbox/vector-tile"; import Protobuf from "pbf"; if (process.argv.length < 3) { console.error("Usage: node list-layers.js "); process.exit(1); } const path = process.argv[2]; const source = new PMTiles(path); await source.open(); // opens the file (or HTTP URL) const header = await source.getHeader(); const { minzoom, maxzoom } = header; // Grab a tile that is guaranteed to exist – zoom 0 is the safest. const tile = await source.getTile(0, 0, 0); if (!tile) { console.error("No tile at z=0/x=0/y=0 – maybe the archive starts at a higher zoom."); process.exit(1); } // Decode the PBF const pbf = new Protobuf(tile.data); const vt = new decode(pbf); const layers = Object.keys(vt.layers); console.log(layers.join("\n")); await source.close(); ``` Run it: ```bash node list-layers.js mydata.pmtiles ``` You’ll get the same list as the `vt2geojson` command. > **Why we fetch zoom 0** – The top‑level tile always contains *all* layer names (even if the tile itself has no features). If your archive starts at a higher zoom (e.g. `minzoom: 5`), fetch any tile at that minzoom instead (`pmtiles tile mydata.pmtiles 5/0/0`). --- ## 5️⃣ Spot‑check a real tile (optional but handy) Pick a zoom where you know there is data, fetch the tile, and turn it into GeoJSON: ```bash # Example: zoom 14, tile x=8580, y=5712 (covers a part of London) pmtiles tile mydata.pmtiles 14/8580/5712 > tile.pbf # Convert to GeoJSON (all layers) vt2geojson tile.pbf > tile.geojson ``` Open `tile.geojson` in any viewer (e.g. `geojson.io`) to confirm that attributes, geometry types, and layer names look correct. --- ## 6️⃣ Serve the file locally for a quick visual test The CLI ships a tiny HTTP server that knows how to answer range requests and also serves a **TileJSON** endpoint for the `url:` source style. ```bash pmtiles serve mydata.pmtiles # → Listening on http://127.0.0.1:8080 ``` Now point a MapLibre style at it: ```js import * as pmtiles from "pmtiles"; import maplibregl from "maplibre-gl"; const protocol = new pmtiles.Protocol(); maplibregl.addProtocol("pmtiles", protocol.tile); new maplibregl.Map({ container: "map", style: { version: 8, sources: { mytiles: { type: "vector", url: "pmtiles://http://127.0.0.1:8080/mydata.pmtiles" } }, layers: [ { id: "water", type: "fill", source: "mytiles", "source-layer": "water", paint: { "fill-color": "#a0c8f0" } }, // …other layers using the same source ] }, center: [0, 0], zoom: 2 }); ``` If the map renders correctly, you’re ready to upload the file. --- ## 7️⃣ Upload & final CORS / cache‑control checklist | Setting | Recommended value | |---------|-------------------| | **`Cache‑Control`** | `public, max-age=31536000, immutable` (if the file will never change) | | **`Access‑Control‑Allow‑Origin`** | `*` (or your domain) | | **`Accept‑Ranges`** | Must be `bytes` – all S3‑compatible hosts provide this automatically. | | **`Content‑Type`** | `application/octet-stream` (or `application/vnd.pmtiles` if you prefer) | Most static hosts (S3, Cloudflare R2, Netlify, Vercel, GitHub Pages) let you set these headers either via the UI or a small `metadata.json`/`.htaccess` file. After upload, run a final sanity check: ```bash curl -I https://my.cdn.com/mydata.pmtiles # Look for: # Accept-Ranges: bytes # Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * # Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable ``` If the headers are correct, the browser will be able to issue range requests without CORS errors. --- ## TL;DR – One‑command checklist ```bash # 1️⃣ Verify integrity pmtiles verify mydata.pmtiles # 2️⃣ Show header / metadata pmtiles show mydata.pmtiles # 3️⃣ List vector layers (requires vt2geojson) pmtiles tile mydata.pmtiles 0/0/0 | vt2geojson --layers # 4️⃣ (Optional) Spot‑check a tile pmtiles tile mydata.pmtiles 14/8580/5712 > tile.pbf && vt2geojson tile.pbf | head # 5️⃣ (Optional) Serve locally for visual testing pmtiles serve mydata.pmtiles ``` If all three commands succeed and the layer list matches what you expect, you can safely upload the `.pmtiles` file to your static host and reference it in MapLibre with the

Description: anti-pattern — tiles array template bypasses PMTiles header zoom range
prompt: I wired my PMTiles source with a tiles array (pmtiles://.../{z}/{x}/{y}) instead of url, and past a certain zoom the tiles go blank. The file is fine in pmtiles show. Why?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
### TL;DR You used a **`tiles:` array** (`pmtiles://…/{z}/{x}/{y}`) instead of a **`url:`** reference. When MapLibre sees a `tiles:` array it **does not read the PMTiles header**, so it has no idea what zoom levels actually exist in the archive. It therefore assumes the default `maxzoom: 22`. As soon as the map asks for a zoom that is **higher than the archive’s real max‑zoom**, the PMTiles protocol still receives a request for a tile that simply isn’t stored, and it returns an empty tile → you see blanks. Switching to `url:` (or adding the correct `minzoom`/`maxzoom` yourself) fixes the problem. --- ## What’s happening under the hood | Property | What MapLibre does | What the PMTiles protocol expects | |----------|-------------------|-----------------------------------| | **`url:`** (e.g. `pmtiles://https://example.com/world.pmtiles`) | Calls the PMTiles protocol handler **once** to fetch a *TileJSON* from the archive’s header. The TileJSON contains `minzoom`, `maxzoom`, `bounds`, `vector_layers`, etc. MapLibre then knows the exact zoom range and can over‑zoom gracefully. | The handler reads the archive header, returns a TileJSON object, and later serves individual tiles via HTTP range requests. | | **`tiles:`** (e.g. `pmtiles://https://example.com/world.pmtiles/{z}/{x}/{y}`) | Treats the value as a *template URL* for raster/vector tiles. **No TileJSON is fetched**; MapLibre falls back to the spec default `maxzoom: 22` (and `minzoom: 0`). | The PMTiles protocol still works for the individual tile requests, but it never sees the archive’s header, so it can’t tell you “this archive only goes to zoom 14”. Requests for zoom 15‑22 hit the archive, find no tile, and return an empty buffer → blank vector tiles (or transparent raster tiles). | ### Why blanks appear only *after* a certain zoom 1. **Zoom ≤ archive‑max** – The tile *does* exist in the file, the range request returns the compressed tile data, and everything renders fine. 2. **Zoom > archive‑max** – The archive has no tile at that level. The protocol returns an empty `ArrayBuffer`. MapLibre interprets that as a valid (but empty) tile, so you get a blank map rather than an error. If you inspect the file with `pmtiles show world.pmtiles` you’ll see something like: ``` minzoom: 0 maxzoom: 14 bounds: -180,-85,180,85 ``` But because you used `tiles:` MapLibre never reads those numbers. --- ## How to fix it ### 1. Use the `url:` property (recommended) ```json { "type": "vector", "url": "pmtiles://https://example.com/world.pmtiles" } ``` *The PMTiles library will automatically:* * fetch the header → produce a TileJSON with the correct `minzoom`/`maxzoom` * serve individual tiles via range requests when the map asks for them ### 2. If you really need a `tiles:` array, add the zoom limits yourself ```json { "type": "vector", "tiles": [ "pmtiles://https://example.com/world.pmtiles/{z}/{x}/{y}" ], "minzoom": 0, "maxzoom": 14 // <-- must match the archive header } ``` *Note:* You must keep these numbers in sync with the archive; otherwise you’ll re‑introduce the blank‑tile problem when the archive changes. ### 3. (Optional) Enable over‑zooming manually If you want MapLibre to “over‑zoom” (i.e., reuse the highest‑available tiles for higher zoom levels) you can set `maxzoom` to the archive’s max and let MapLibre handle the over‑zoom. With a `url:` source this happens automatically; with a `tiles:` source you must also set `maxzoom` correctly. ```json { "type": "vector", "url": "pmtiles://https://example.com/world.pmtiles", "maxzoom": 14, // optional – MapLibre will read it anyway "overzoom": true // (MapLibre v4+ does this by default) } ``` --- ## Quick checklist for a healthy PMTiles source | ✅ | Item | |---|------| | **Protocol registration** | `maplibregl.addProtocol('pmtiles', new pmtiles.Protocol().tile);` (once, before any map is created) | | **Source definition** | Use `url:` **or** `tiles:` **plus** correct `minzoom`/`maxzoom`. | | **CORS & Range support** | Host must return `Access‑Control‑Allow‑Origin: *` (or your domain) and `Accept‑Ranges: bytes`. | | **Cache headers** | `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000` (if the file is immutable). | | **File integrity** | `pmtiles verify world.pmtiles` → no errors. | | **Zoom range sanity** | `pmtiles show world.pmtiles` → note `minzoom`/`maxzoom` and make sure they match the style source. | --- ## Example – Full minimal setup ```html PMTiles with MapLibre
``` *If you ever need to switch to a `tiles:` array (e.g., for a custom tile‑URL pattern), just add the explicit `minzoom`/`maxzoom` that you saw with `pmtiles show`. Otherwise stick with `url:` – it’s the simplest and most robust way.* --- ### TL;DR Recap * **Problem:** `tiles:` array bypasses the PMTiles header → MapLibre assumes a default max‑zoom (22) → requests zoom levels that don’t exist → blank tiles. * **Solution:** Use `url:` (`pmtiles://…/file.pmtiles`) so the protocol can read the header, or manually set `minzoom`/`maxzoom` when you must use `tiles:`. Once you make that change, the map will render correctly at all zoom levels that the archive actually contains, and over‑zoom will work automatically. Happy mapping!
